'''Naum Natanovich (Nokhim Sanalevich) Meiman'''  ({{langx|ru|Нау́м Ната́нович (Но́хим Са́нелевич) Ме́йман}}; 12 May 1912, [[Bazar, Ukraine]] – 31 March 2001, [[Tel Aviv]]) was a Soviet [[mathematician]], and [[Soviet dissidents|dissident]].<ref name=obituary>{{cite journal |last1= Anosov|first1=D.V.|last2= Ginzburg|first2= V.L.|last3=Zhizhchenko|first3=A.B.|last4=Monastyrskii|first4=M.I.|last5=Novikov|author-link5=Sergei Novikov (mathematician)|first5=S.P.|last6=Sinai|first6=Ya.G.|last7=Solov’ev|first7=M.A.|year= 2002|title= Naum Meiman. Obituary|journal= Russ. Math. Surv.|volume= 57|issue= 2|pages= 399&ndash;405|bibcode=2002RuMaS..57..399A|doi= 10.1070/RM2002v057n02ABEH000499|s2cid=250837995 }}</ref> He is known for his work in [[complex analysis]], [[partial differential equations]], and [[mathematical physics]], as well as for his dissident activity, in particular, for being a member of the [[Moscow Helsinki Group]].

==Life==
He was born in [[Bazar, Ukraine]] on 12 May 1912.<ref name=obituary/> In 1932 he graduated from [[Kazan State University]] as an [[extern]]. In 1937 he submitted his Ph.D. under the supervision of [[Nikolai Chebotaryov]] and was awarded the degree [[Doktor nauk]]. In 1939 he became a full professor at [[Kazan State University]].<ref name="obituary"/>

He worked for two years in the Mathematics Institute at the [[University of Kharkiv]], where he became friends with [[Lev Landau]] with whom he collaborated for many years. After the Second World War, he went to [[Moscow]] and worked at the [[Institute for Physical Problems]], where he was a head of the mathematics lab. Then he worked in the [[Institute for Theoretical and Experimental Physics]]. In 1953, he was awarded a [[USSR State Prize|Stalin prize]] for his work in [[theoretical physics]]. He made important contributions in the development of [[nuclear weapons]] in the USSR.
<!-- Deleted image removed: [[File:Meiman dissidents.gif|left|thumb|315px|[[Soviet dissidents]] in 1977. Back row: Meiman, [[Sofiya Kallistratova]], [[Petro Grigorenko]], his wife Zinaida Grigorenko, [[Tatyana Velikanova]]'s mother, the priest Sergei Zheludkov and [[Andrei Sakharov]]; front row: Genrikh Altunyan and [[Alexander Podrabinek]].<ref>{{cite book|author=Подрабинек, Александр|script-title=ru:Диссиденты|trans-title=Dissidents|date=2014|publisher=АСТ|location=Moscow|isbn=978-5-17-082401-4|language=ru}}</ref>{{ffdc|1=Meiman dissidents.gif|log=2022 April 15}}]] -->

Starting in 1968, Meiman became active in politics and signed several letters of protest against political trials in the [[USSR]].<ref name="obituary" />

In 1971, he retired and applied for permission to emigrate to Israel. Denied on grounds of knowing state secrets, he soon became a [[refusenik]]. Gradually he became more active in politics, and was a member of the [[Moscow Helsinki Group]] beginning in 1977. Later he became deputy chairman and the last active free member, writing hundreds of the group's documents. He also participated in a Refusenik scientific seminar. He was permanently under surveillance by the [[KGB]], who also bugged his telephone and searched his home.

In 1982, Naum Meiman and [[Andrei Dmitrievich Sakharov]] published a letter in defence of [[Yuri Fyodorovich Orlov]].<ref>{{cite journal|author1=Sakharov, Andrei |author2=Meiman, Naum |title=The plight of Yuri Orlov|journal=[[Harvard International Review]]|date=March–April 1982|volume=4|issue=6|pages=50|jstor=42762207}}</ref>

Meiman also struggled for the right of his wife [[Inna Meiman-Kitrossky]] to go to the USA for medical treatment since she had been diagnosed with cancer. After several years of struggle, she was allowed to go to the US and she died in February 1987 in [[Georgetown (Washington, D.C.)]].<ref>{{cite book  | last = Paul  | first = Lisa  | title = Swimming in the Daylight: An American Student, a Soviet-Jewish Dissident, and the Gift of Hope  |url = http://www.goodreads.com/book/show/10295308-swimming-in-the-daylight| publisher = Skyhorse Publishing | year = 2011 | isbn = 978-1-61608-203-1}}</ref><ref>{{YouTube|sseV26HziPc|Lisa Paul presents her book}}</ref><ref name="stonov">{{cite web|url=https://www.angelfire.com/sc3/soviet_jews_exodus/English/Chronicle_s/Stonov_Review.shtml|title=Book review|author= Leonid Stonov|publisher= Association «Remember and save»|access-date=2011-02-23}}</ref> Meiman was not allowed to attend her funeral in Washington D.C.<ref>{{cite journal|author=Saxon, Wolfgang|title=Inna Meiman, emigre, dies at 53; left Soviet for cancer treatment|journal=[[The New York Times]]|date=10 February 1987|url=https://www.nytimes.com/1987/02/10/obituaries/inna-meiman-emigre-dies-at-53-left-soviet-for-cancer-treatment.html}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal|author=Taubman, Philip|title=Old and alone, Soviet dissident looks to exit|journal=[[The New York Times]]|date=26 February 1987|url=https://www.nytimes.com/1987/02/26/world/old-and-alone-soviet-dissident-looks-to-exit.html}}</ref>

In 1988 Meiman was finally allowed to emigrate to Israel, where he became a professor emeritus in [[Tel Aviv University]]. In 1992, in Tel-Aviv, there was a conference in his honor dedicated to his 80th birthday. Meiman died there in 2001.<ref name="obituary" />
